title: The Seventh Day and the Garden in Eden
summary: God finishes his work, rests on the seventh day, and blesses and sanctifies it. The story then turns close up: the LORD God forms the man from the dust, breathes life into him, and places him in a garden in Eden to work it and keep it, with one tree forbidden. Finding no suitable partner among the animals, God builds a woman from the man's side, and the chapter closes with the first marriage and a couple naked and unashamed.
story:
Genesis 1 showed the whole world from above. The first three verses here finish that account with a day unlike the others, a day with no work and no closing evening. Then, from verse 4, the camera comes down to ground level. The God who spoke galaxies into place now kneels in the dirt to shape a man, plants a garden, gives him work and a word to obey, and notices that something is not yet good. The chapter sets up everything the next one will break: the trees, the command, the man and the woman, their trust, and their unashamed openness to each other and to God. Readers who know how chapter 3 goes will feel the weight of verse 17 and verse 25.

Verse 4 also opens the first of the ten sections of Genesis marked by the heading ‘This is the account of’ (toledot). The account of the heavens and the earth runs through chapter 4, and it tells not how the heavens and earth began but what came of them: a garden, a family, and then a fracture that spreads.
historical:
Verse 4 introduces the first of the recurring headings that divide Genesis, “This is the account of” (in Hebrew, elleh toledot, literally ‘these are the generations of’). The noun toledot comes from the verb to bear or beget, and it occurs thirteen times in Genesis, ten of them as section headings (2:4, 5:1, 6:9, 10:1, 11:10, 11:27, 25:12, 25:19, 36:1, 37:2, with a repetition at 36:9). Each heading names a starting point and then tells what came from it, so the account of Terah is mostly about Abraham, and the account of Jacob is mostly about Joseph. Here, uniquely, the starting point is not a person but the heavens and the earth. Scholars debate whether 2:4a closes chapter 1 as a summary or opens chapter 2 as a heading; the pattern elsewhere in Genesis, where the formula always introduces what follows, favors the second, and the chiastic shape of the whole verse (heavens and earth, created; made, earth and heavens) binds its two halves together.

The same verse brings a new name for God: the LORD God. In most English Bibles LORD in small capitals stands for the personal name of Israel's God, written YHWH in Hebrew and probably pronounced something like Yahweh, which he later explains to Moses (Exodus 3:14-15). Chapter 1 used only the general word for God. The compound LORD God occurs twenty times in 2:4-3:24 and only once more in the whole Pentateuch (Exodus 9:30). Many critical scholars take this change, along with differences in style and order, as a sign that 2:4b-3:24 comes from a different and possibly older source than chapter 1, usually called the Yahwist or simply non-priestly material. Others, including Umberto Cassuto (The Documentary Hypothesis, Hebrew 1941, English 1961), argued that the names are chosen for their meaning: God the Creator of all in chapter 1, and the LORD, the covenant God personally near to his people, in chapters 2 and 3.

The geography of verses 10 to 14 mixes the familiar and the unknown. The Hiddekel is the Tigris and the Perat is the Euphrates, the two rivers of Mesopotamia. The Pishon and the Gihon cannot be identified with confidence. Cush elsewhere usually means the land south of Egypt (ancient Nubia), though some scholars suggest the Kassite region of Mesopotamia here, and Havilah is usually placed in Arabia. Gihon is also the name of Jerusalem's spring (1 Kings 1:33, 2 Chronicles 32:30). Proposals for Eden's location range from the head of the Persian Gulf to the mountains of eastern Turkey. The name itself has two candidate backgrounds: a Sumerian and Akkadian word for the open steppe (edin), or the Semitic root for abundance and delight. Alan Millard (Vetus Testamentum, 1984) pointed to the ninth-century BC Aramaic inscription from Tell Fekheriye, where the storm god is praised as the one who makes the land luxuriant with water using that root, and proposed that Eden means a well-watered place. The text places Eden at the source of the world's great rivers without letting it be found on a map.
cultural:
Ancient kings planted gardens, walled parks of trees and water that displayed their power, and temples often had gardens. Readers have long noticed that Eden is described in the language Israel later used for its sanctuary, an argument developed especially by Gordon Wenham. God walks there (3:8), using the reflexive form of the verb (mithallek) later used for his presence in Israel's camp and tabernacle (Leviticus 26:12, Deuteronomy 23:14, 2 Samuel 7:6-7). Gold and onyx, the materials of the land beside the garden, reappear in the tabernacle and on the high priest's garments, where two onyx stones carry the names of the tribes (Exodus 28:9-12). The two verbs of verse 15, to work or serve (avad) and to keep or guard (shamar), are paired again for the Levites' care of the tabernacle (Numbers 3:7-8). Cherubim guard Eden's eastern entrance (3:24), as woven cherubim mark the veil of the holy place, and the tabernacle faced east. A river flows out of Eden, as Ezekiel later sees a river flowing from the temple (Ezekiel 47:1) and the psalmist sings of a river that makes glad the city of God (Psalm 46:4). Ezekiel 28:13-14 even calls Eden “the garden of God” and places it on “the holy mountain of God”. On this reading Eden is the first sanctuary and the man its first priest as well as its gardener.

The making of the man also speaks into its world. Neighboring peoples told of humans formed from clay: in the Babylonian Atrahasis epic clay is mixed with the blood of a slain god, and Egyptian art shows the ram-headed god Khnum shaping people on a potter's wheel. Genesis uses a potter's verb too (yatsar, the word behind yotser, potter, in Jeremiah 18), but the man is formed from humble dust and receives God's own breath. Made of the same stuff as the ground, he is yet alive with a life that comes directly from God. The wordplay of Hebrew helps: the man is adam, taken from the adamah, the ground, and the woman is ishshah, taken from ish, man. The two pairs are wordplay rather than etymology (ish and ishshah probably come from different roots), but the sound carries the meaning. The Sumerian myth Enki and Ninhursag offers a curious parallel in Eden-like Dilmun: to heal the god Enki's rib the goddess brings forth Ninti, a name that can mean both ‘lady of the rib’ and ‘lady who makes live’. Samuel Noah Kramer suggested this pun lies far behind the rib and the name Eve, though in Hebrew the words for rib and life have nothing in common.

Marriage customs lie behind verses 22 to 24. A bride was brought to the groom, usually by her father; here God himself brings her. The man's exclamation, “bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh”, uses a kinship formula that elsewhere binds relatives and allies (Laban to Jacob in Genesis 29:14, the tribes to David in 2 Samuel 5:1), and Walter Brueggemann argued (Catholic Biblical Quarterly, 1970) that it expresses covenant loyalty as much as common substance. In Israel it was normally the wife who left her father's household, so verse 24's picture of the man leaving father and mother is striking; most read it as a statement of loyalty rather than residence. Naming also carried authority in that world: Pharaoh renamed Eliakim, and Nebuchadnezzar renamed Mattaniah (2 Kings 23:34, 24:17).
literary:
The chapter has two parts. Verses 1 to 3 close the seven-day account with its own threefold rhythm: the seventh day is named three times in three clauses of seven Hebrew words each, and the paragraph has thirty-five words in all. It ends without the familiar evening and morning, as if the seventh day stays open. Verses 4 to 25 are a single narrative that moves from lack to fullness. It opens with a list of what is missing (no shrub, no plant, no rain, no man to work the ground) and closes with a man, a woman, a garden, and nothing hidden between them.

The viewpoint differs from chapter 1. There God speaks and things appear in a cosmic sequence; here the LORD God forms, breathes, plants, takes, puts, commands, brings, and builds, verbs of a craftsman and a host. The man is at the center, and the narrative is arranged around his needs: ground and work (verses 5 to 15), a word to live by (16 and 17), and a companion (18 to 25). Inside that frame the narrator builds suspense with a surprising sentence, “It is not good for the man to be alone” (verse 18), the first thing in Genesis called not good after the sevenfold good of chapter 1. The parade of animals delays the answer and teaches the man what he lacks, and the deep sleep keeps the making of the woman God's secret. The climax is the man's first recorded words, a short poem of delight in verse 23 in which the word ‘this’ (zot) occurs three times. Verse 24 steps outside the story to draw a lesson for every later reader, and verse 25 quietly sets the stage for chapter 3: naked (arummim) is nearly the same word as the serpent's craftiness (arum) in the next verse.

The chapter also plants the vocabulary of the next. The tree of the knowledge of good and evil, the command, the verb eat, the phrase “in the day that you eat of it”, the pair of adam and adamah, and nakedness without shame all return in chapter 3, reversed.

outline.t: God rests on the seventh day and makes it holy
The LORD God forms the man and gives him breath
The garden in Eden and its four rivers
Work to do and a command to keep
Not good to be alone: the man names the animals
The woman, the first marriage, and no shame

doctrines.note: The first thing God blesses and sanctifies in the Bible is not a place or a person but a day (verse 3). God does not rest from weariness but because the work is complete, and he builds rest into the created order before there is any law. Exodus 20:11 grounds Israel's weekly Sabbath here, and Hebrews 4 sees in the unending seventh day a rest God still offers his people.

Human beings are dust and breath together: creatures made from the ground and dependent on it, yet given life by God's own breath (verse 7). The chapter also shows that humans were made for relationship; solitude is the first thing God calls not good. Man and woman share one nature (bone of my bones) and stand before God as partners.

Marriage appears here as God's gift, a man and a woman leaving their parents and being joined into one flesh. The woman is a partner who corresponds to the man, and the chapter ends with a union marked by trust and the absence of shame. Jesus returns to this passage as the pattern for marriage (Matthew 19:4-6), and Paul reads it as a picture of Christ and the church.

Work appears in the garden before anything goes wrong. The man is placed in Eden to cultivate it and keep it (verse 15), and he names the animals, an act of understanding and care. Labor is part of the good life God designed; what chapter 3 adds is not work but toil and frustration.

Eden is described with the vocabulary of Israel's sanctuary: God walking there, gold and onyx, a river flowing out, the paired verbs of priestly service, and (in 3:24) cherubim at an eastern entrance. The garden is the first place where God dwells with people, the pattern the tabernacle, temple, and new Jerusalem will echo.

words.note: Shavat, to cease or stop, often translated rested in verses 2 and 3. It occurs about seventy times, often simply for something coming to an end (the manna ceased, Joshua 5:12; day and night will not cease, Genesis 8:22). The word is not about recovering from tiredness but about stopping because the work is complete. The noun Sabbath comes from the same root, and Exodus 20:11 and 31:17 ground Israel's weekly day of rest in this verse, while Deuteronomy 5:15 adds a second ground, the rescue from slavery in Egypt.

Toledot, generations, account, family history. It occurs thirty-nine times, thirteen of them in Genesis, where it marks the book's main divisions, and elsewhere mostly in genealogies (Numbers 1, 1 Chronicles). From the verb yalad, to bear or beget, it means what is produced from a starting point. Ruth 4:18 uses the same heading for the line from Perez to David, and the Greek of Matthew 1:1 (‘the book of the genesis of Jesus Christ’) echoes the heading of Genesis 5:1, a sign that the Gospel means to open a new chapter in the same story.

Yatsar, to form, fashion, shape, the verb of the potter (the participle yotser means potter in Jeremiah 18:2-6). It occurs about forty times, especially in Isaiah 40 to 49, where God forms Israel as his servant (Isaiah 43:1, 44:2, 44:24) and the idol makers form worthless images (44:9-12). Here it is used of the man (verses 7 and 8) and the animals (verse 19). The picture is of hands-on craftsmanship, and it lets the text say both that humans are frail clay and that they are shaped with personal care.

Neshamah, breath. It occurs twenty-four times, always of the breath of God or of living beings, never of wind alone. In verse 7 God breathes the breath of life (nishmat chayyim) into the man's nostrils. The word appears again in Job 32:8 and 33:4, where the breath of the Almighty gives understanding and life, and in Proverbs 20:27, where the human breath or spirit is the lamp of the LORD. The Greek Septuagint uses the verb emphysaō for God's breathing here, and John 20:22 uses the same verb, found only there in the New Testament, when the risen Jesus breathes on his disciples.

Nephesh, usually translated soul, but here in the phrase living being (nephesh chayyah). The word occurs more than seven hundred times with a wide range: throat, appetite, life, person, self. The same phrase describes the animals in 1:20-24, so it does not mean a separate immortal part inside the body. It names the whole living, breathing creature. What sets the man apart in this verse is not the word nephesh but the personal breath of God that makes him one.

Ezer, helper, help. Modern ears can hear this as an assistant or subordinate, but of its twenty-one occurrences in the Hebrew Bible about sixteen refer to God as the helper of his people (for example Exodus 18:4, Deuteronomy 33:29, and Psalm 121:1-2); the others refer to military allies. The word describes help that supplies what is lacking, and it says nothing by itself about rank. Paired with kenegdo, literally ‘corresponding to him’ or ‘opposite him’ (from neged, in front of), it presents the woman as the man's true counterpart.

Tsela, rib or side. It occurs about forty times, and outside this chapter never of a body part: it names the sides of the ark of the covenant and the tabernacle (Exodus 25:12, 26:20), the side rooms and planks of Solomon's temple (1 Kings 6:5, 6:15), and the side of a hill (2 Samuel 16:13). Many interpreters therefore read ‘side’ here, as the Septuagint's pleura allows, and some rabbis in Genesis Rabbah 8:1 took it that way. Either way the woman is built (banah, a builder's verb) from the man's own body, sharing his nature.

Davaq, to cling or hold fast, translated be united in verse 24. It occurs about fifty-five times, used of a tongue sticking to the roof of the mouth (Psalm 137:6), of Ruth clinging to Naomi (Ruth 1:14), and especially in Deuteronomy and Joshua of Israel holding fast to the LORD (Deuteronomy 10:20, 30:20, Joshua 23:8). Here it describes the loyal, lasting bond of marriage, which is why the verse pairs it with leaving (azav) father and mother, the language of covenant loyalty.

christ:
Jesus quotes this chapter when he is asked about divorce. He joins Genesis 1:27 and 2:24 and concludes, “So they are no longer two, but one flesh. Therefore what God has joined together, let man not separate” (Matthew 19:6), appealing to God's design ‘from the beginning’ over later concessions made because of hardness of heart (Matthew 19:8). Paul quotes the same verse and adds, “This mystery is profound, but I am speaking about Christ and the church” (Ephesians 5:32), so that marriage becomes a living picture of Christ's self-giving love for his people. Many of the church fathers, Augustine among them, saw a further pattern: as the woman was taken from the side of the sleeping Adam, so the church was born from the side of Christ in the sleep of death, from which blood and water flowed (John 19:34). That is a typological reading, a pattern noticed, not a claim the Genesis text makes.

Paul also takes up verse 7. Adam received breath and became a living being; the risen Christ is “the last Adam a life-giving spirit” (1 Corinthians 15:45), and “The first man was of the dust of the earth, the second man from heaven” (1 Corinthians 15:47). The one who received life is contrasted with the one who gives it. John tells the same story in narrative: on Easter evening the risen Jesus breathes on his disciples and gives them the Holy Spirit (John 20:22), using the verb the Greek Old Testament used for God breathing into Adam, a new creation beginning in the old one.

The seventh day is picked up in Hebrews 4. Because God's rest has no closing evening, the writer can say “There remains, then, a Sabbath rest for the people of God” (Hebrews 4:9), a rest entered by faith in Christ. The garden returns at the Bible's end. The Greek word for the garden, paradeisos, gives the name Paradise, which Jesus promises to the dying thief (Luke 23:43) and the risen Christ promises to those who overcome (Revelation 2:7). Revelation 22 shows a river of the water of life flowing from the throne of God and the Lamb and the tree of life beside it, in a city where God dwells with his people. The garden-sanctuary of Genesis 2 becomes the pattern of the final home. These are the New Testament's own readings, not codes hidden in Genesis 2.
interpretation:
Jewish interpretation filled in what the chapter leaves open. The Book of Jubilees (second century BC) says the man was brought into the garden after forty days and the woman after eighty, matching the purification periods of Leviticus 12, so that Eden is treated as holier than any other ground. Philo of Alexandria (Allegorical Interpretation 1.31) distinguished the heavenly man made in the image in Genesis 1 from the earthly man molded of clay here. Genesis Rabbah 8:1 records Rabbi Jeremiah ben Eleazar teaching that the first human was created androgynous, and Rabbi Samuel bar Nahman that God made the first human with two faces and then sawed it in two, reading tsela as side. On the helper, the Talmud (Yevamot 63a) records Rabbi Eleazar's play on kenegdo: if a man is worthy, his wife is a help; if not, she is against him, a reading Rashi repeats. In worship the chapter's opening verses are among the best known in Judaism: Genesis 2:1-3 (Vayechulu) is recited in the Friday evening prayer and opens the Kiddush, the blessing over wine that begins the Sabbath at home. Abraham Joshua Heschel's The Sabbath (1951) built on verse 3 his argument that the first thing the Bible calls holy is time, so that the Sabbath is a sanctuary in time.

Christian interpreters asked what the woman's creation says about her dignity. Augustine (The Literal Meaning of Genesis, book 9) argued that she was made a helper chiefly for bearing children, a view later readers have criticized as too narrow. Peter Lombard's Sentences and Thomas Aquinas (Summa Theologiae I, question 92, article 3) drew a lesson that became proverbial: the woman was taken not from the man's head, as if to rule him, nor from his feet, as if to be his servant, but from his side, as a companion. Luther and Calvin both honored marriage from this chapter against the medieval ranking of celibacy above it. Milton's Paradise Lost (1667) gave the garden, Adam's loneliness, and Eve's first awakening their most famous English form.

Modern readers have pressed the chapter from several sides. Source critics read 2:4b-25 as a second creation account; Umberto Cassuto and later literary critics such as Robert Alter read the two chapters as a deliberate composite. Elizabeth Cady Stanton's Woman's Bible (1895) contrasted the equality of 1:27 with what she saw as the afterthought woman of chapter 2. Phyllis Trible (God and the Rhetoric of Sexuality, 1978) answered that the first adam is a sexually undifferentiated earth creature and that man and woman emerge together in verses 21 to 23. Karl Barth found in the man and woman the relational form of the image of God, and Pope John Paul II's Wednesday audiences on the theology of the body (1979 to 1984) began from this chapter's original solitude, unity, and nakedness. Evangelical scholars continue to divide over whether the order of creation implies male headship, a debate traced in the hard questions.

In the church's liturgy verses 18 to 24 are a common wedding reading, and the Revised Common Lectionary pairs them with Jesus' teaching on divorce (Mark 10:2-16) in Year B. In art, Michelangelo's Creation of Eve sits at the center of the Sistine ceiling, and medieval bestiaries and manuscripts often show Adam naming the animals.
text:
English Bibles differ at several points in this chapter.

In verse 2 the standard Hebrew (Masoretic) text reads that God finished his work on the seventh day. The Septuagint, the Samaritan Pentateuch, and the Syriac version read ‘on the sixth day’, removing any hint that God worked on the seventh. Most scholars judge the Hebrew original, the harder reading that a scribe would be tempted to smooth; many translations render it ‘by the seventh day God had finished’ (as the BSB does) or treat the verb as pluperfect.

In verse 4 translations divide the verse differently. Some print 4a as the close of chapter 1 and begin a new paragraph at 4b (NRSV, NJPS), while others keep the verse together as a heading (BSB, ESV, NIV). The choice reflects the source-critical debate noted above.

The rare word ed in verse 6 (found only here and in Job 36:27) is rendered ‘mist’ (KJV, ESV), ‘streams’ (NIV), or “springs” (BSB), since its meaning is uncertain; many connect it with an Akkadian word for flood or subterranean water.

In verse 8 the Septuagint translated garden as paradeisos, a Persian loanword for an enclosed royal park, which through Latin became paradise; the Vulgate read miqqedem in its time sense, ‘from the beginning’, where most versions read ‘in the east’. In verse 19 the verb formed can be rendered as a pluperfect, ‘had formed’ (NIV), which removes the apparent conflict with the order of Genesis 1; most versions keep a simple past. Translations also differ on where the man first becomes the proper name Adam: Hebrew writes ha'adam, ‘the man’, through most of chapters 2 and 3, and the form without the article in verse 20 can be read either way, so some versions introduce Adam at 2:20 and others not until 3:17 or later. In verse 24 the Septuagint adds ‘the two’ (and the two shall become one flesh), the form in which Jesus and Paul quote it (Matthew 19:5, Ephesians 5:31). The verse numbers are the same in Hebrew and English Bibles.

teach.big: God finishes his good world with holy rest, then forms human beings from dust and breath for work, obedience, and one-flesh companionship in his presence.

outline.t: God's work is finished, and he blesses and sanctifies a day of rest; rest is a gift woven into creation before it is a command.
The covenant LORD shapes the man from dust and breathes life into him: we are humble creatures and yet alive with God's own gift.
God plants a garden, a well-watered place of beauty, food, and his presence, from which life flows out to the world.
The man is given work to do and one command to keep, set inside overwhelming generosity; freedom and limits belong together.
Solitude is the first thing God calls not good, and the man learns by naming the animals that none of them corresponds to him.
God builds the woman and brings her to the man, and marriage is formed by leaving, holding fast, and one flesh, with no shame.

teach.pitfalls:
Several misreadings recur. The first treats chapter 2 as a contradiction of chapter 1 or, from the other side, forces the two into a single timeline at every point; better to let each do what it does, one the cosmic frame and the other the close-up story. The second reads helper as inferior and uses the word to justify domineering husbands. The word is used most often of God, and nothing in it makes the woman less than the man; whatever one concludes about order in marriage (see the hard questions), the text cannot be used to belittle women. The third reads not good to be alone as a verdict that single people are incomplete. The problem named is human isolation, which God meets in many ways; Jesus and Paul were single, and the church is meant to be a family for everyone.

A fourth pitfall reduces the Sabbath to a rule about which day to keep, missing that it is first God's own rest and blessing. A fifth reads the command of verses 16 and 17 as a trap or a test God expected to be failed. It comes wrapped in abundance (every other tree freely given) and teaches that life with God is life under his word. Finally, avoid making the garden merely a lost golden age to be nostalgic about. The Bible treats it as the pattern of God's purpose, which the story moves toward, not only away from.
teach.pastoral: This chapter presses on people who are lonely, single, divorced, or in painful marriages. Teach not good to be alone as God's compassion toward isolation, not as a judgment on the unmarried, and point to the church as the household where no one should be alone. Verse 24 and Jesus' use of it will sting for the divorced; hold up God's design without making them the target, and remember that Jesus spoke against a hardness of heart that often belonged to the one who left. Where there is abuse, be clear that one flesh never obliges anyone to remain in danger, and that helper and holding fast describe loyalty and love, never permission to harm. The closing picture of nakedness without shame will touch people who carry sexual shame; it tells them what God intended and what his grace restores.

hard.q: Does Genesis 2 contradict Genesis 1 on the order of creation?
hard.a:
The objection is strong on its face. Genesis 1 has plants on day three, animals on day six, and humanity last, male and female together. Genesis 2 begins with no plants yet, forms the man, then plants a garden, then forms the animals (verse 19), and finally makes the woman. The name of God, the style, and the picture of God also change. Since Julius Wellhausen in the nineteenth century, most critical scholars have concluded that two accounts from different sources have been placed side by side, and popular presentations such as Richard Elliott Friedman's Who Wrote the Bible? (1987) make the two creation stories a leading example. Elizabeth Cady Stanton (The Woman's Bible, 1895) asked why one book should contain two contradictory accounts of the same event, and many skeptics still cite the chapter as proof that the Bible contradicts itself.

Responses come in several forms. Many critical scholars, while holding to two sources, argue that the editor who joined them saw no contradiction because each account makes its own theological point, the first cosmic and the second human and intimate. Umberto Cassuto (Hebrew 1941, English 1961) and later literary critics such as Robert Alter argued that the difference of names and styles is deliberate and that ancient narrative often sets a general account beside a detailed one. Readers who hold to a single author offer specific solutions: the shrub and plant of the field in verse 5 may mean the wild scrub and cultivated grain that need rain and human work, not all vegetation, a point Meredith Kline (1958) and Mark Futato (Westminster Theological Journal, 1998) developed; and the verb in verse 19 can be rendered had formed, as the NIV does, describing animals already made rather than a new order of creation. On this view chapter 2 zooms in on the sixth day and arranges events by theme. Faithful readers differ on which of these explanations is best; both critical and conservative scholars agree that the final form of Genesis presents the chapters as complementary.

hard.q: Does the order of creation in Genesis 2 make the woman subordinate to the man?
hard.a:
The strongest objection comes from feminist readers who see the chapter as the charter of patriarchy: the man is made first, the woman is made from him and for him as a helper, and he names her. Elizabeth Cady Stanton called her an afterthought, and many critics since have argued that the story reflects and justifies the male-centered household of ancient Israel. Some Christian readers draw a milder but related conclusion: Paul cites the order of creation in 1 Corinthians 11:8-9 (“For man did not come from woman, but woman from man”) and 1 Timothy 2:13 (“For Adam was formed first, and then Eve”), and complementarian scholars, such as Raymond Ortlund Jr. in Recovering Biblical Manhood and Womanhood (edited by John Piper and Wayne Grudem, 1991), argue that Genesis 2 establishes male headship in marriage before the fall, exercised in love, alongside full equality of worth.

Other readers answer differently. Phyllis Trible (1978) argued that the first human is not yet male and that the story builds to the woman as its climax. Egalitarian scholars, such as Richard Hess in Discovering Biblical Equality (2004), note that ezer is used most often of God, that kenegdo means corresponding to, not beneath, and that the rule of husband over wife first appears in 3:16 as a consequence of sin rather than a creation ordinance. Paul himself adds in the same passage that in the Lord woman is not independent of man nor man of woman, “For just as woman came from man, so also man is born of woman” (1 Corinthians 11:12). Traditional Jewish commentary, from the Talmud to Rashi, generally assumed the husband's authority while praising the wife's help. The question of roles in marriage and church is a second-order one on which faithful Christians disagree; what all agree the chapter teaches is that man and woman share one nature, stand together before God, and were made for each other without shame.

observe: What is missing at the start of the story (verses 5 and 6), and what has been supplied by the end (verse 25)?
List what the LORD God does in this chapter. Which verbs describe him as a craftsman, a gardener, or a host?
What is the first thing called not good, and what steps does God take before he meets the need?
interpret: Why does God rest on the seventh day, and why might this day have no closing evening and morning?
What does the word helper mean, given that the Old Testament most often uses it of God?
What details suggest that Eden is pictured as a sanctuary, and what difference does that make for understanding the man's work?
apply: The first thing God calls not good is the man being alone. What does that say about how you were made, and about the isolation many people live with?
Work appears in the garden before anything goes wrong. How might it change your view of your daily work to see it as part of the good life God designed?
God blesses a day of rest before there is any law commanding it. What would it take for you to receive rest as a gift rather than something to earn?
